result.summary: Pausanias describes the temple of Athene Alea at Tegea, its statues, relics and altar, the nearby race-course and spring, and other Tegean sanctuaries. He gives local legends about Athene Poliatis protecting the city and about Artemis Hegemone and Aristomelidas.

scenes.title: Temple of Athene Alea
scenes.summary: Pausanias lists the statue, offerings, altar, race-course and spring at the Tegean temple of Athene, and the nearby temple of Hermes.

scenes.title: Athene Poliatis and Medusa's lock
scenes.summary: The temple of Athene Poliatis is entered by the priest once a year; Athene gave Cepheus a lock of Medusa to keep Tegea safe.

scenes.title: Artemis Hegemone legend
scenes.summary: Aristomelidas seizes a Tegean maiden, who kills herself. Artemis sends Chronius a dream, he kills the tyrant and founds her temple at Tegea.
scenes.stakes: The maiden's honour and life; Aristomelidas's life.

alias_notes.explanation: Title of Athene used by most Greeks; Manthurii call her Hippia.
Cult title of Hermes at Tegea.

analysis.text: Sacred objects and local legends tie Tegea's identity to Athene, its war victories and its protection from capture.
The fetters and the Halotia games commemorate Tegea's capture of Spartan prisoners, a point of civic pride against Sparta.

fun_facts.text: The Calydonian boar hide was a famous relic at Tegea, which Pausanias saw decayed with age.

language_notes.text: Alludes to the Gigantomachy, the gods' war against the giants; Enceladus was one giant, and Hippia means 'of the horse' or chariot.
The Calydonian boar was the monster hunted by Meleager and others; its hide was a famous relic kept at Tegea.
Halotia derives from the Greek word for 'captured', referring to the Lacedæmonian prisoners taken in battle.
Auge was priestess of Athene and mother of Telephus by Hercules; Hecatæus was an early historian who told her story differently.
Medusa was the Gorgon whose severed head Athene bore; her hair was a talisman, here guarding the city.
"Somehow or other" is Pausanias' vague way of saying he does not know how the maiden was seized.

context_notes.text: Scopas of Paros was a celebrated fourth-century BC sculptor who worked on temples at Tegea; Æsculapius is the healing god and Hygiea his daughter, Health.
Melampus was a legendary Greek seer and healer, credited with founding various cults and rites.
Poliatis means 'protectress of the city'; the restricted entry shows the shrine's special sanctity.
Artemis Hegemone means 'Artemis the Leader'; the tale gives an origin for her cult at Tegea.

literary_notes.text: Medusa's lock stands for divine protection: a dreadful object turned into a talisman guaranteeing the city's safety.
The maiden's suicide shows her virtue and fear in a single brief clause, giving the tyrant's lust a tragic result.
